text: So far you've added and changed rows. Now you'll remove them entirely with DELETE FROM.

DELETE FROM removes entire rows from a table -- it never names columns, because you can't delete part of a row, only the whole thing. This removes every row where Color equals Discontinued, leaving every other row untouched.

Just like UPDATE, omitting WHERE is legal and removes every row in the table. The table itself still exists afterward -- its columns, constraints, and IDENTITY definition are unchanged -- but it now has zero rows.

Because DELETE is permanent and has no built-in preview, run the same condition as a SELECT first to see exactly which rows will disappear. Look, then act -- that's the single best protection against deleting the wrong rows.

DELETE can also use a join to decide which rows to remove based on a second table. Here, rows in dbo dot LessonDemo are deleted wherever the matching real product's ProductLine is not R. The alias goes right after DELETE, the same shape you saw with joined UPDATE.
Next, you'll compare DELETE to TRUNCATE TABLE -- two different ways to empty a table.
